subject: feral goats
title: What If Goats Ate an Island? The Galapagos Fought Back With Traitor Goats

scenes.text: What if goats ate a whole island? In the Galapagos they nearly did. The fix was traitor goats.
Settlers brought goats in the 1800s. With no predators, they multiplied past 100,000 and stripped the islands bare.
Giant tortoises, already hunted from over 250,000 down to about 3,000 by the 1970s, now lost their food too.
From 1999, sharpshooters in helicopters removed 90 percent of the goats. The survivors hid in caves and lava tunnels.
So rangers released Judas goats: sterilised, radio-collared, dosed with hormones to stay in heat. Goats seek company. The collars led hunters to every hidden herd.
Seven years, over 140,000 goats and ten million dollars later, the forest grew back and tortoises returned. The Judas goats are nearly the only ones left.

description:
What if goats ate an island? Feral goats brought to the Galapagos by settlers stripped the vegetation that giant tortoises needed, and tortoise numbers fell from over 250,000 to about 3,000 by the 1970s.
Project Isabela (1997 to 2006) removed more than 140,000 goats with helicopter marksmen and then Judas goats, sterilised, hormone-treated animals with radio collars that led hunters to the last hidden herds. It cost about 10.5 million dollars; vegetation and tortoises have recovered.

first_comment: It was the largest island restoration project ever attempted. About 770 Judas goats were used on Isabela alone, and 266 were kept there in 2006 to catch any newcomer. Which invasive species should we run through next?
